headline.text: Sending $1,000 to India today: a Chase wire loses ₹3,580, Remitly loses ₹121, the USDC via Solana route lands ₹2,518 above mid-market even after tax. Here's every hop.

sources.label: Mid-market USD/INR (median of four keyless feeds)
sources.note: Median of Wise's mid-market rate, Coinbase's exchange-rates endpoint, open.er-api.com and the ECB reference rate via Frankfurter. ECB and ExchangeRate-API update once per working day, so on weekends the median leans on the two live feeds. Every route is measured against this one number.

sources.label: Wise public comparison feed (USD to INR)
sources.note: Keyless endpoint that powers wise.com/compare. Each provider quote carries its own collection timestamp, which can be up to a few days old for banks. Wise runs this feed and is itself a competitor in it, so we recompute every markup against our own mid-market median instead of using Wise's markup figure.

sources.label: CoinDCX public order books (USDC/INR, USDT/INR, USDC/USDT)
sources.note: Keyless order book endpoint. We market-sell the full amount into the bid side, level by level, so larger transfers pay for thin books. Top 50 bid levels are stored in each snapshot.

sources.label: Base gas price and L1 data fee
sources.note: eth_gasPrice times 65,000 gas for a USDC transfer, plus the L1 data fee upper bound from the GasPriceOracle predeploy (0x4200...000F) for a 300 byte transaction.

sources.label: Solana base fee and recent priority fees
sources.note: 5,000 lamport base fee plus the 75th percentile of getRecentPrioritizationFees for the USDC mint, over a 30,000 compute unit budget.

sources.label: ETH and SOL spot prices in USD
sources.note: Used only to convert network fees into dollars.

sources.label: Chase outgoing international wire, sent in USD, online
sources.publisher: JPMorgan Chase, Additional Banking Services and Fees (personal), corroborated by Monito
sources.note: Chase charges $40 for a USD-denominated international wire sent online ($50 with a banker) and $5 (or $0 at $5,000 and above) when sent in foreign currency. The foreign-currency fee is confirmed live by the Wise feed ($5 at $1,000, $0 at $5,000). Chase's personal fee page moved and its old URL returns 404, so the $40 figure is cited from independent 2026 fee guides and dated the day it was last checked. Re-check against Chase's Deposit Account Agreement.

sources.label: Correspondent (intermediary) bank deduction on a USD SWIFT wire
sources.note: Banks disclose that intermediaries "may deduct" fees but do not publish amounts. $20 is a mid-range assumption for one intermediary on a SHA wire. This is the least certain number in the model, and it only affects the "SWIFT in USD" route.

sources.label: Coinbase ACH deposit fee
sources.note: Standard ACH deposits into a US Coinbase account are free (last checked 2026-10-04). Wire deposits cost $10. ACH takes several business days to clear before the USDC can be sent.

sources.label: Coinbase USD to USDC conversion fee
sources.note: Coinbase converts USD to USDC 1:1 with no fee or spread (last checked 2026-10-04). Coinbase Exchange charges on USDC to USD conversions above $2 million per 30 days, irrelevant here.

sources.label: Crypto deposit fee on CoinDCX
sources.note: Deposits are free. Check that the exchange accepts USDC on the network you send on before sending: support varies by token and network.

sources.label: CoinDCX INR market taker fee
sources.publisher: Assumption based on CoinDCX's published fee page
sources.note: Indian exchanges publish INR-market spot fees in the 0.1% to 0.5% range depending on tier and promotions. We use 0.5% (the conservative end). The fee page blocks automated access, so this is not fetched live: re-check before publishing.

sources.label: CoinDCX USDC/USDT market fee
sources.publisher: Assumption based on CoinDCX's published fee page
sources.note: Only used on the USDC to USDT to INR path. Assumed 0.1%.

sources.label: INR withdrawal fee to an Indian bank account
sources.note: Assumed ₹10 flat per IMPS withdrawal. Several 2026 fee guides list CoinDCX INR withdrawals as free, so this is deliberately conservative. Immaterial at these amounts.

sources.label: GST on currency conversion, Rule 32(2)(b) of the CGST Rules, 2017
sources.note: When a bank converts foreign currency, GST at 18% applies to a deemed value: 1% of the gross amount up to ₹1 lakh (minimum ₹250), ₹1,000 plus 0.5% of the amount above ₹1 lakh up to ₹10 lakh, ₹5,500 plus 0.1% of the amount above ₹10 lakh (value capped at ₹60,000). This slab method is Rule 32(2)(b), an option the bank may elect instead of the spread-based Rule 32(2)(a). Banks apply it to inward USD remittances they convert. It does not apply when the money arrives already in INR, which is why provider routes skip it.

sources.label: GST on exchange fees
sources.note: Exchange trading fees are a taxable service at the standard 18% (9% CGST + 9% SGST, or 18% IGST). Indian exchanges add it on top of the fee.

sources.label: 1% TDS on transfer of virtual digital assets
sources.publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India (Section 194S; CBDT Circular 13/2022)
sources.note: Introduced by the Finance Act, 2022 as Section 194S of the Income-tax Act, 1961, and carried into the Income-tax Act, 2025 under new numbering; we cite the 1961 section because exchanges and CBDT guidance still use it. The exchange withholds 1% on every VDA transfer, including crypto to crypto swaps. Per CBDT Circular 13/2022 the base is the consideration excluding GST and the exchange's own charges, so the model withholds on proceeds net of fee and GST. No TDS is due if the year's total is under ₹10,000 (₹50,000 for a "specified person"); the model always withholds. TDS is credited against your tax, or refunded, only when you file your return.

sources.label: 30% tax on income from transfer of virtual digital assets, plus 4% cess
sources.publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India (Section 115BBH, Finance Act 2022)
sources.note: Section 115BBH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (carried into the 2025 Act): gains are taxed at a flat 30%, only the cost of acquisition is deductible (no fees), and losses cannot be set off against anything. 4% health and education cess applies on top. Surcharge at high incomes is ignored. We assume a cost basis equal to the mid-market INR value of the USDC, which is the right model when you are moving your own money or a gift from a relative. If the USDC is payment for services, it is taxed as income on receipt instead.

sources.label: Health and education cess on income tax
sources.publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India (Finance Act, 2018)
